title: Helio Health Security Review — Runtime LTS support window / vuln response / SBOM
next_steps: Redwood to share draft LTS vulnerability response SLA language (security patch turnaround + notification process).
Redwood to provide sample LTS artifact bundle (checksums + provenance/attestation + SBOM example) for Helio security review.
Helio to confirm whether they require offline/air-gapped SBOM delivery for Private and if CycloneDX is preferred over SPDX.
Schedule a follow-up with Helio Platform Eng to walk through Private installer pinning/rollback flow for LTS patches.

Dr. Aisha Rahman - Provide Redwood vulnerability management overview (intake, triage, disclosure, advisory process) tailored to LTS - Due 2025-02-18
Connor O'Brien - Share example of LTS release notes with CVE section + backport rationale and risk rubric - Due 2025-02-18
Sahana Iyer - Export a sample SBOM/provenance/checksum bundle from an internal LTS RC artifact - Due 2025-02-19

topics: Runtime LTS support window and patch cadence (monthly + out-of-band security)
Vulnerability response: severity definitions, SLAs, disclosure/notification, backport policy
SBOM format, provenance/attestations, artifact signing and checksum verification
Auditability: mapping release artifacts to commits, reproducible builds, change control evidence

summary: Helio Health security/compliance team reviewed Redwood’s planned Runtime LTS channel expectations: support window (~12 months), patch cadence (monthly) and an out-of-band path for security fixes. Helio requested specifics on vulnerability response SLAs for LTS (triage + patch timelines), how Redwood will provide SBOMs and provenance for LTS artifacts, and how releases can be audited (artifact-to-commit traceability, signing, and change control evidence). Redwood committed to share sample LTS release artifacts (checksums + SBOM + provenance) and draft contract-ready language for security patch commitments and customer notification.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-02-13
Start time: 19:02 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Title: Helio Health Security Review — Runtime LTS support window / vuln response / SBOM
Attendees (Redwood): Avery Johnson, Dr. Aisha Rahman, Hanae Suzuki, Connor O'Brien, Sahana Iyer
Attendees (Helio Health): Priya Nair, Daniel Cho, Megan Alvarez, Tom Kline

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
Questions:
- What is the vulnerability response SLA specifically for the LTS runtime line?
- Do you provide SBOMs for runtime artifacts? In what format (SPDX/CycloneDX)?
- How do you sign artifacts and provide provenance/attestation?
- How do customers verify an LTS artifact maps to a specific commit and approved change list?

Transcript

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This one is mostly for security review on our upcoming runtime LTS channel. Priya, Daniel, thanks for bringing the list. We have Aisha and Hanae from security, Connor from release engineering, Sahana from CI and build.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Yep, thanks Avery. We’re in the middle of doing vendor risk for the Private deployment plus the LTS thing you guys mentioned. A lot of our concern is, like, what happens when there’s a vuln and we’re pinned for twelve months, right?

[00:34] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Makes sense. We can cover the response process and what’s different for LTS versus your normal release train.

[00:42] Daniel Cho: And we also need evidence artifacts for audit. Like SBOM, signature, provenance, and ideally something we can show change control. We’re healthcare so, you know, we get audited.

[00:55] Avery Johnson: Yep. Maybe Connor can start with what we mean by LTS support window and patch cadence, then Aisha/Hanae on vuln response.

[01:04] Connor O'Brien: Sure. So the LTS channel, the plan is: we cut a branch off a mainline runtime release, say runtime-1.18-lts. That branch is supported for at least 12 months from first patch GA. During that period we do predictable patches, currently targeting monthly. And then security fixes can be out-of-band if needed.

[01:30] Megan Alvarez: When you say monthly, is that like a fixed Tuesday, or it’s “sometime in the month”?

[01:36] Connor O'Brien: The goal is a consistent week. We’re aiming for “second week of the month” for patch publish, but with the caveat of perf gates and validation. We’d communicate dates ahead of time and publish release notes.

[01:52] Priya Nair: Okay. Now the big question: vulnerability response. If there’s a CVE in some dependency, what’s the SLA? And do we get notified? Because with some vendors it’s like, you discover it on Hacker News.

[02:08] Hanae Suzuki: Yeah, so we have a vulnerability intake and response program. For LTS specifically, we’re defining a security patch SLA and notification workflow. Today for our hosted services we respond fast, but you’re asking about Private + pinned artifacts.

[02:24] Dr. Aisha Rahman: The way we structure it is severity-based. Critical and high severity issues that are exploitable in our runtime or shipped components qualify for a backport into the LTS line. And then we’ll publish an advisory and deliver a patched artifact.

[02:43] Daniel Cho: Can you be more concrete? Like, “critical within X days.” We need something contractable.

[02:51] Avery Johnson: Yeah, totally fair. We have draft language, not final, but we can share what we’re targeting.

[02:58] Dr. Aisha Rahman: What we’ve been aligning on internally: for critical security issues impacting LTS customers, patch availability target is 72 hours for an out-of-band fix, assuming we have a confirmed repro and a safe patch. For high severity, we target within 7 calendar days, sometimes rolling into the next scheduled patch if it’s within that window.

[03:22] Priya Nair: That’s helpful. And notification? Email? Portal?

[03:26] Hanae Suzuki: Notification is two paths. One is direct customer notification via your support contacts and CSM if you’re in Private/Dedicated. The other is a published advisory. For some issues there’s coordinated disclosure timing.

[03:40] Daniel Cho: You’ll publish CVE references? Or is it just “security update”?

[03:45] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We’ll reference CVEs when applicable. Sometimes it’s a non-CVE issue, like a logic flaw, but we still do an advisory ID. For LTS release notes we include a “Security” section with advisory IDs, impacted versions, fixed versions, and mitigation if patching is delayed.

[04:06] Megan Alvarez: If we’re air-gapped-ish—like we can pull artifacts but we have to stage them—do we get the advisory + artifact in a package? Because we can’t rely on web pages being accessible in prod.

[04:18] Connor O'Brien: For Private we can provide a release bundle that includes the images, checksums, release notes in a file, and metadata. We’re also adding SBOM/provenance artifacts per release.

[04:31] Priya Nair: Great, that brings me to SBOM. Do you provide SBOMs today? What format? We prefer CycloneDX JSON.

[04:39] Sahana Iyer: We provide SBOMs for some artifacts today and we’re standardizing it for the runtime LTS builds. The plan is to generate SBOMs as part of the release CI workflow and ship them alongside the artifacts.

[04:52] Priya Nair: Sorry if this is basic—SBOM for container image? Or for the binaries inside?

[04:58] Sahana Iyer: Good question. The practical answer is SBOM for the container image, which includes the OS packages plus our runtime binaries and dependencies. We can also generate a component-level SBOM for the runtime build output, but most customers consume the image SBOM.

[05:15] Daniel Cho: Is it SPDX or CycloneDX?

[05:18] Sahana Iyer: We can produce CycloneDX. Internally we’ve been testing CycloneDX JSON. SPDX is doable too, but we’ve leaned CycloneDX for enterprise requests.

[05:30] Priya Nair: And provenance. Do you do SLSA attestation? Like, can we verify the build came from your CI and from a specific git commit?

[05:40] Connor O'Brien: That’s the direction. For LTS we’re adding provenance metadata that ties the artifact to a commit SHA, build ID, and build workflow. Think “attestation” you can verify.

[05:53] Daniel Cho: Are you signing with cosign? Or GPG?

[05:57] Sahana Iyer: We’re using cosign for container signatures and attestations. For checksums we publish SHA-256. We can also provide a signature over the checksum file.

[06:08] Priya Nair: Can we verify offline? Like, we download the bundle, verify signature, and then we’re done.

[06:14] Sahana Iyer: Yes, that’s the goal. You’d have our public key or certificate chain, verify the signature and the attestations locally.

[06:22] Megan Alvarez: I’m going to ask a dumb operational question. If there’s an out-of-band security patch, does that break the “monthly predictable” cadence? Because our change window is monthly.

[06:34] Avery Johnson: That’s a common tension. The LTS channel is stable, but security can force an emergency. We generally recommend customers treat critical security patches as exceptions and have an expedited change path.

[06:48] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And we’ll provide mitigations when possible. For example, if it’s a dependency that’s only used in a specific configuration, we’d document configuration-level mitigation, but we can’t always.

[07:02] Daniel Cho: Okay. What about “mandatory vs optional” patches? Some vendors mark patches as mandatory.

[07:08] Connor O'Brien: We expect most monthly patches to be optional, but security and severe correctness issues can be “recommended” or “mandatory”. The criteria is tied to severity and exploitability. If it’s a confirmed exploited-in-the-wild issue, we’d mark it mandatory.

[07:28] Priya Nair: Can you define “severity” for runtime? Like if it’s a crash but only for certain prompts, is that Sev1? Or is it security only?

[07:36] Connor O'Brien: For LTS we have a backport rubric. Separate from security, Sev1 correctness or crash issues that impact production workloads qualify. Performance regressions can also qualify if they breach thresholds.

[07:52] Priya Nair: I’m going to keep this security-focused: if a vuln is in a base image, do you rebuild and push a patched base image under the same runtime version? Or do you bump the patch version?

[08:03] Sahana Iyer: We bump the patch version. We don’t mutate existing tags. For auditability we don’t overwrite artifacts. So you’d see 1.18.2-lts, 1.18.3-lts, etc. Each has its own checksums and attestation.

[08:19] Daniel Cho: Good. Immutable is important. We’ve had vendors quietly repush.

[08:25] Megan Alvarez: How do we pin? Like in Helm values, do we specify the exact 1.18.3-lts tag?

[08:32] Connor O'Brien: Yes. For Private/Helm we support pinning to a specific patch. The installer also verifies checksums.

[08:41] Priya Nair: And what’s the support window exactly? You said “at least 12 months.” Is it exactly 12 months? Could it be longer? We need predictable end-of-life.

[08:52] Avery Johnson: The plan we’ve been communicating is 12 months standard, with the option to extend for some enterprise contracts. But we want to set a clear baseline first.

[09:02] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We will publish EOL dates per LTS branch. So you’ll know the last date we’ll ship patches and advisories for that line.

[09:14] Daniel Cho: If you find a critical vuln after EOL, do you patch? Or is it “upgrade to next LTS”?

[09:21] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Generally, after EOL we’d recommend upgrading to a supported LTS. For specific contractual cases we can discuss extended support, but default is: supported window only.

[09:34] Priya Nair: Okay. On the audit side, we need to show: “these were the changes included, approved, and tested.” How do your release notes look for LTS? Are they detailed?

[09:45] Connor O'Brien: LTS release notes are “slower-change.” We categorize: Security, Critical Fixes, Reliability, Performance, Packaging, Known Issues. Each item references the commit/PR, and we include compatibility matrix and upgrade notes.

[10:03] Daniel Cho: Do you include a list of dependencies versions? Like OpenSSL, glibc, whatever.

[10:08] Sahana Iyer: We can. That tends to be in the SBOM. The release notes call out notable dependency updates, especially security-driven ones.

[10:18] Megan Alvarez: And reproducible builds—do you guarantee reproducible builds? Or just that you provide provenance.

[10:25] Connor O'Brien: “Reproducible” is a spectrum. For LTS we’re focusing on deterministic build steps and traceability. We can’t guarantee anyone can rebuild byte-for-byte in their environment today, but we can provide build metadata and commit mapping, and we’re moving toward more reproducibility.

[10:44] Priya Nair: That’s fine. We mostly need provenance and that you’re not doing manual builds on someone’s laptop.

[10:50] Sahana Iyer: Yeah, for LTS releases it’s CI only, with controlled credentials. Signing keys are managed with limited access.

[11:00] Daniel Cho: Who has access to the signing keys? And do you rotate?

[11:06] Sahana Iyer: We restrict access to the release automation service account. Human access is limited, and we have rotation policies. I can provide a written summary of key management controls (not the secrets obviously).

[11:18] Priya Nair: Great. Another question: do you provide SOC 2 and ISO reports? Sorry, separate but related.

[11:24] Avery Johnson: Yes, we have SOC 2 Type II. We can share under NDA via our trust portal.

[11:29] Daniel Cho: Okay.

[11:32] Priya Nair: Back to vuln response: do you scan your images? Like do you have a vulnerability scanner running on every release? And do you block releases on criticals?

[11:42] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We do automated scanning. For LTS, we’re increasing strictness: critical vulnerabilities in shipped components should block release unless there’s a documented exception and mitigation. The exception process is rare.

[11:58] Daniel Cho: If there’s a critical in a dependency but it’s not reachable, do you still block?

[12:03] Hanae Suzuki: We evaluate reachability and exploitability, but we still tend to patch. For enterprise we’ll document the rationale either way.

[12:14] Megan Alvarez: Slight tangent: we’ve seen performance regressions with some model serving stacks when they change kernels. Is your LTS line freezing kernel stuff?

[12:24] Connor O'Brien: Yes, the whole point is stability in kernels and scheduling. We freeze certain autotune defaults and avoid experimental heuristics in the LTS branch. If we must change something for a security fix, we note perf impacts.

[12:41] Priya Nair: That’s good, but for security review I care if a patch changes behavior and we don’t know.

[12:47] Connor O'Brien: That’s why the release notes are detailed and we gate with perf and regression tests.

[12:54] Daniel Cho: Can you describe the “gates”? Not too deep, but enough for audit.

[13:00] Connor O'Brien: Sure. Each patch has: unit/integration tests, targeted scheduler regression tests, plus a perf canary suite. And we require sign-off from Release Eng and Runtime and SRE for anything high risk.

[13:16] Priya Nair: Is there a waiver process? Because perf tests can be noisy.

[13:21] Connor O'Brien: There is, but it’s documented. Waivers require explicit approval and are reflected in the release notes as “known variance.”

[13:33] Megan Alvarez: If we adopt LTS, do we still have to upgrade mainline for new features? Like tool calling stuff.

[13:39] Avery Johnson: LTS is stability-first. If you need newest features, mainline hosted might be better. For Private, most customers pick LTS and accept slower features.

[13:50] Priya Nair: Okay. Let’s get specific on artifacts. For Private deployment, what do you actually deliver? Is it a Helm chart pointing to images, or do you ship a tarball?

[14:02] Connor O'Brien: Both options. Most customers use Helm with a registry pull. For restricted environments, we support exporting images and providing checksums. The LTS release bundle includes: image digests, SHA256 checksums, SBOM(s), provenance/attestation, and release notes.

[14:23] Daniel Cho: And the release notes include the git SHA?

[14:26] Connor O'Brien: Yes, and tags.

[14:29] Priya Nair: Great. Also, audit logs. For Hosted we’d want audit logs; for Private, we need logs of admin actions. Do you have audit logs in the control plane?

[14:41] Avery Johnson: For Hosted and Dedicated, we have audit logs for console actions, API key events, and config changes. For Private, we provide audit logging options and can integrate with your SIEM, depending on deployment mode.

[14:56] Megan Alvarez: But if it’s Private and we manage the cluster, are the logs in our cluster? Or are you phoning home.

[15:02] Avery Johnson: No forced phone-home. In Private, you control networking; we can run fully within your environment. Audit logs would be emitted locally, and you can forward.

[15:14] Priya Nair: Thank you. We have strict no-egress in some segments.

[15:18] Dr. Aisha Rahman: On security advisories, if there’s no egress, we can provide notifications through your designated contacts. That’s more process than tech.

[15:28] Daniel Cho: Another compliance item: we need an SBOM retention policy. Like, do you keep SBOMs accessible for the full support window? Sometimes vendors delete old stuff.

[15:38] Connor O'Brien: For LTS we intend to keep artifacts and metadata available for the duration of support, plus an archive period after EOL. We can specify retention in documentation.

[15:51] Priya Nair: Okay. Can we get a sample SBOM and attestation file? That would help our tooling team test verification.

[15:58] Sahana Iyer: Yes. We can generate one from an internal RC build and share it. It’ll be representative.

[16:07] Megan Alvarez: Another question, sorry, on CVE remediation. If the vuln is in, like, Ubuntu base packages, do you rebuild the whole stack or just patch the layer.

[16:17] Sahana Iyer: We rebuild the image in CI using updated base layers. We do not do “manual apt-get in prod”. It’s a clean build.

[16:29] Daniel Cho: And do you document exactly which packages changed?

[16:33] Connor O'Brien: Usually via the SBOM diff and release notes callouts.

[16:40] Priya Nair: How do you handle coordinated disclosure? If you patch before disclosure, do we get notified privately?

[16:47] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes, for impacted enterprise customers we can do pre-notification under embargo, depending on the issue and your ability to keep it confidential.

[17:00] Daniel Cho: We can handle embargo.

[17:02] Avery Johnson: Good.

[17:05] Priya Nair: What about third-party pen test results? Do you share? Usually vendors say no.

[17:12] Avery Johnson: We share summaries via our trust portal. Full reports are typically under NDA and limited.

[17:18] Priya Nair: That’s fine.

[17:21] Megan Alvarez: I want to confirm rollback. If we patch from 1.18.2-lts to 1.18.3-lts and something breaks, can we roll back quickly?

[17:30] Connor O'Brien: Yes. Part of LTS is clear rollback guidance. Since tags are immutable, rollback is pinning back to the prior patch version. We also note any data-plane compatibility concerns.

[17:45] Priya Nair: Are there any state migrations?

[17:48] Connor O'Brien: Generally runtime is stateless, but there are config changes sometimes. Release notes include upgrade notes.

[17:58] Daniel Cho: Okay. Switching back to audit: approvals. Who approves a security patch? Is there an on-call? Is it “two-person rule”?

[18:09] Hanae Suzuki: For emergency LTS security patches, we require approval from Security and the runtime owner plus release manager. There’s a documented exception path for time-critical issues, but still multiple approvers.

[18:27] Priya Nair: And do you maintain an incident record? Like, if there was a security incident.

[18:33] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Yes, we have an incident management process. For customer-impacting security issues we provide postmortems as appropriate.

[18:43] Megan Alvarez: This is helpful. I know this is a security call, but can I ask: the LTS line won’t include new features, right? We want to avoid surprise changes.

[18:52] Connor O'Brien: Correct. Only security and critical fixes. We avoid feature backports.

[19:00] Daniel Cho: Could a “critical fix” change behavior though.

[19:03] Connor O'Brien: It can, but the rubric is to keep diffs minimal and to document risk. That’s why we require targeted tests.

[19:12] Priya Nair: Okay. Do you have a public policy doc? Like “LTS backport policy.”

[19:18] Avery Johnson: We’re drafting it. We can share the draft and incorporate your feedback.

[19:23] Priya Nair: Please do.

[19:25] Daniel Cho: Another audit question: do you provide an “artifact manifest” listing digests, checksums, sizes, etc.

[19:33] Sahana Iyer: Yes, that’s part of the bundle. It’s basically a manifest file. We can include image digest, tag, build timestamp, commit SHA.

[19:45] Daniel Cho: Great.

[19:47] Priya Nair: Also, we use our own scanning pipeline. We want to ingest your SBOMs but also scan ourselves. Any restrictions?

[19:55] Avery Johnson: No restrictions.

[19:57] Dr. Aisha Rahman: And if you find something, we’d like to get it through our vuln intake.

[20:03] Priya Nair: Yep.

[20:05] Megan Alvarez: If you guys have a “trust portal”, can we access as part of the evaluation? Or only after contract.

[20:12] Avery Johnson: We can grant access under NDA during evaluation.

[20:18] Tom Kline: Procurement here. Just confirming, the SLA language—can we get it soon? Our legal process is slow.

[20:25] Avery Johnson: Yes, we’ll send draft language for the LTS security patch SLA and support window by tomorrow.

[20:32] Daniel Cho: One more technical question: do you keep a list of known vulnerabilities accepted? Like a risk acceptance register.

[20:41] Dr. Aisha Rahman: We do internally. For customers, we can disclose exceptions when they affect shipped artifacts, including mitigations.

[20:52] Priya Nair: Okay.

[20:54] Megan Alvarez: Can you talk about logging and audit in Private? If you’re not calling home, how do you do license checks, etc.

[21:03] Avery Johnson: Private is licensed but not dependent on runtime egress. We can do offline license files.

[21:10] Megan Alvarez: Okay good.

[21:12] Priya Nair: I think we have what we need. But I want to be explicit: we need proof you can produce SBOM and provenance for LTS artifacts.

[21:22] Sahana Iyer: Understood. We’ll send a sample bundle. It might have some redactions but the structure will be real.

[21:30] Daniel Cho: And please include verification steps. Like how to validate cosign, how to check the SHA.

[21:36] Sahana Iyer: Yep, we’ll include a short “verify” doc.

[21:41] Avery Johnson: Great. Before we wrap, Aisha, anything else we should highlight about vuln response for LTS.

[21:48] Dr. Aisha Rahman: Just that LTS does not mean “no patches.” It means controlled patches. Security fixes are prioritized. We’ll provide advisories and clear remediation guidance.

[21:59] Priya Nair: Perfect.

[22:01] Avery Johnson: Recap next steps: we’ll send draft SLA language, we’ll send a sample SBOM/provenance bundle and a sample LTS release note, and then schedule a follow-up focused on Private pinning and rollback. Sound good?

[22:14] Megan Alvarez: Yep.

[22:15] Daniel Cho: Works.

[22:16] Priya Nair: Thanks.

[22:18] Avery Johnson: Thanks everyone.

(Transcript continues with a few minutes of side questions about NDA access and scheduling; audio overlap and minor crosstalk.)

[47:03] Priya Nair: Sorry last thing—do you guys call it “S-bomb” or “S-bom”?

[47:07] Sahana Iyer: [laughs] SBOM. We say “S-bom.”

[47:10] Priya Nair: Great.

[47:12] Avery Johnson: Alright, we’ll follow up in email. Thanks all.
